**4B.8 Research Note**
Kishida’s 2024 behavior is strongly consistent with respect for succession and constitutional transfer. The clearest direct evidence is his August 14 decision to step aside and support a transparent LDP leadership contest, followed by the cabinet’s collective resignation on October 1. The main negative signal is political bargaining with conservatives to stay in power earlier in the year, but the sources describe that as coalition management, not rule-breaking or refusal to transfer power.

- [Prime Minister to step aside for LDP presidential race](https://www.investing.com/news/economy-news/japan-pm-kishida-wont-run-for-reelection-at-ldp-race-kyodo-reports-3570455) | Reuters | August 14, 2024 | Reuters reported that Kishida would not run again and said stepping aside was the clearest first step to show the LDP was changing. This is strong evidence that he accepted succession rather than trying to entrench himself. | Question IDs: 4B.8

- [Press Conference by Prime Minister Kishida](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202408/14kaiken.html) | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | August 14, 2024 | Kishida said the upcoming LDP presidential election should be transparent, with free and vigorous debate, and that he would support the successor chosen by vote. This is direct evidence of respecting internal succession rules. | Question IDs: 4B.8

- [Press Conference by Prime Minister Kishida](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202408/06kaiken.html) | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | August 6, 2024 | Kishida said the LDP committee should decide the election date and format in a neutral and fair manner, and that an open presidential election was desirable. This supports a finding that he did not try to manage succession as a closed or sham process. | Question IDs: 4B.8

- [Remarks by Prime Minister Kishida at the 79th UN General Assembly](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202409/0928enzetsu.html) | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | September 28, 2024 | Kishida framed Japan’s foreign policy around the UN Charter, human dignity, and lawful international order. While not about domestic succession, it is consistent with constitutionalist and rule-bound transfer norms. | Question IDs: 4B.8

- [Cabinet Resignation Ceremony / Remarks by Prime Minister Kishida](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202410/1001danwa.html) | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | October 1, 2024 | Kishida said the cabinet resigned en masse. That is direct evidence of the ordinary constitutional transfer of executive office after the leadership change. | Question IDs: 4B.8

- [AP report on Kishida’s political survival](https://apnews.com/article/05926b50f4f5a83a631f779d906cf06d) | Associated Press | September 30, 2024 | AP said Kishida compromised with conservative nationalists to stay in power. This is mixed evidence: it suggests coalition bargaining and political survival tactics, but it does not show refusal to step down, manipulation of succession rules, or constitutional violations. | Question IDs: 4B.8

- [AP report on Kishida’s exit and coalition context](https://apnews.com/article/05926b50f4f5a83a631f779d906cf06d) | Associated Press | September 30, 2024 | The same AP piece notes Kishida improved ties with partners and then left under pressure. That supports the view that succession occurred through standard political turnover rather than coercive retention. | Question IDs: 4B.8

**Search gap**
I found no credible 2024 evidence that Kishida violated term rules, blocked a successor, refused to transfer authority, or interfered with Japan’s constitutional transfer of power. The only negative material was coalition compromise and political survival, which is not the same as succession-rule abuse.
